SmartOps: Model Results, Python Code & Reproducibility

Explore our model experiments, performance comparisons, interactive visualizations, and complete Python analysis with executed Google Colab results.

View the Python code & executed Colab results ↓Start with the model results

We ran 99 model configurations from 9 families to predict whether an engine needs maintenance from six sensor readings. Each family below explains how the model works, the variations we tried, and the score each variation got. The short version: once a model can bend its curves, they all land in the same place, about 0.70 AUC.

Results come first. Below them, the Code Appendix holds the executed Google Colab notebook (every code cell with its real output and charts) and all the Python code behind the saved experiments. This file is the final submission version.

Before the details

How to read the scores

ROC AUC

Pick one engine that needs maintenance and one that doesn't. AUC is the chance the model gives the first one the higher risk score. 0.50 is a coin flip and 1.00 is perfect. Our models sit around 0.70: they rank the right engine higher about 70% of the time.

Cross-validation

Every score comes from the 16,604 training and validation rows, split 5 ways and repeated 3 times (15 fits). Each fit is scored on rows it never saw, and the 15 scores are averaged. The 2,931-row test set was kept aside and used only for the final models.

Fair comparisons

When we tune settings and score on the same folds, the score is slightly flattering. Nested cross-validation tunes inside each training fold instead, so the score is fair. Hollow dots mark the flattering kind. The bias is about 0.001.

Is a difference real?

We compared models fold by fold with a corrected t-test. Almost every gap between the good models was too small to be more than chance.

Applied on top of the models

Other techniques we tested

These are changes to how a model is trained or used, not new model types. None of them improved ranking quality.

Test-set results

Six finalists were scored once on the 2,931 held-out engines. The lines show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. All six are within 0.006 of each other and their intervals overlap almost completely, so on the test set they are tied.

Test AUC95% confidence intervalSelected model (GAM)

What the variations told us

Lessons

  • Bending curves is what matters. Moving from straight-line logistic regression (0.688) to any model with curved effects (about 0.703) is the only big jump in the whole project.
  • Sensor interactions add nothing. Models that can combine sensors (boosting, forests, neural nets) tie models that can't (GAM, naive Bayes). Explicit interaction terms gained +0.0003 to +0.0008, and none was significant. The sensors are close to independent: no pair correlates above 0.09.
  • Tuning matters for boosting, not for additive models. XGBoost went from 0.662 to 0.702 with tuning. Spline and GAM settings move the score by only 0.002.
  • Simpler settings win. Every boosting library chose tiny trees, and deeper CatBoost trees did steadily worse. Engineered features and feature selection made things slightly worse.
  • Combining models doesn't help. They all learn the same additive pattern and make the same mistakes, so averaging gains at most +0.0005.
  • The limit looks like the data, not the algorithm. Nine very different families converge on 0.703 to 0.705, and models that can learn sensor combinations do no better than ones that can't. Bigger gains would most likely need new information: more sensors, readings over time, or cleaner labels.
  • Selected model: the GAM with 20 splines (CV 0.7041, test 0.7095), which is also the model running in the dashboard. It was selected for its competitive cross-validation score, its interpretability (one readable curve per sensor) and its easy implementation (120 coefficients plus knots, evaluated in the browser). It is not claimed to be the most accurate: the spline logistic regression is statistically tied (CV 0.7032, 0.7026 nested; test 0.7099; CV difference +0.0009, p = 0.21; test difference interval contains 0), as is tuned boosting.
What we learned

What the results mean for inspection decisions

SmartOps helps maintenance teams decide which engines to inspect first when inspection capacity is limited. This section turns the model findings into decisions: how to use the risk scores, what the trade-off between false alarms and missed faults looks like, and when a score-based rule is worth using at all.

All cost figures and savings below are hypothetical. The dataset contains no cost information. Costs are expressed in made-up units (one unneeded inspection = 1) to show how the decision changes with the assumption. They are scenarios, not actual or forecast company savings.

1 · The most important findings

  • The ranking is useful but modest. Nine very different model families converge on a cross-validated AUC of about 0.703 to 0.705, and the final models score about 0.71 on the held-out test set (selected GAM 0.7095, 95% CI 0.692 to 0.728; spline logistic regression 0.7099). An AUC of 0.71 means the score ranks engines better than chance, not that it identifies faults reliably.
  • Curved effects matter; interactions and complexity do not. Letting each sensor's effect bend lifts AUC from 0.688 to about 0.703. Boosting, forests and neural nets that can combine sensors do no better than additive models, so a simple, transparent model loses nothing.
  • Engine RPM drives the score. Shuffling RPM costs about 0.147 AUC in the GAM, more than five times any other sensor (fuel pressure about 0.026). Coolant temperature adds almost nothing.
  • The GAM is our selected model, but no single model is proven best. It has the best single cross-validation score (0.7041) and is the model the dashboard runs. We selected it for its competitive score, its interpretability (one readable curve per sensor) and because it is easy to implement in a browser. It differs from the spline logistic regression by 0.0004 test AUC with overlapping intervals, so we claim no superiority.

2 · Risk scores as an inspection priority list

Engines are sorted by predicted risk and inspected from the top. A random pick would find a fault in about 63% of inspections (the share of engines labelled “needs maintenance”), so the useful comparison is the lift over that baseline. Figures come from out-of-fold predictions on the development data (Section K of the executed notebook).

3 · Unnecessary inspections versus missed maintenance cases

Raising the alert threshold flags fewer engines. That cuts unneeded inspections (higher precision, more normal engines left alone) but lets more faults slip through (lower recall). Rows 0.50 and 0.65 are highlighted.

Because 63% of engines need maintenance, flagging everyone already gives recall 1.00 at precision 0.63. A threshold is only worth using if the unneeded inspections it avoids are worth more than the faults it misses, which depends on costs the dataset does not contain.

4 · Threshold and cost sensitivity (hypothetical costs)

One unneeded inspection costs 1 unit. A missed fault costs r units. For each r, the best alert threshold is chosen on the development predictions only, and its expected cost per engine is compared with the two no-model options: inspect every engine, or inspect none.

What the scenarios say

Equal costs (r = 1): the best threshold is about 0.49. It flags roughly 78% of engines and lowers the expected cost by about 11% compared with inspecting every engine.

Missed faults about 3× as costly (r = 3): the score-based rule saves only about 0.03% over inspecting every engine under these assumptions (less than 0.0001 per engine), which is negligible, so inspecting everyone becomes the preferred strategy. At r = 1.5 and r = 2 the saving shrinks to about 3.5% and 1.3%.

“Inspect none” is never the cheapest option in these scenarios.

Sanity check on unseen data: the thresholds were chosen on development data and then applied once to the test set, with no re-tuning.

Rule (chosen on development data only)ThresholdEngines flaggedPrecisionFaults caught (recall)

5 · Inspection capacity changes the decision

  • Capacity, not the threshold, should set how far down the list to go. At the equal-cost threshold of 0.49 the model flags about 78% of engines. A team that can inspect only 30% of them cannot act on that alert list; it should simply work from the top of the ranking.
  • The smaller the budget, the higher the hit rate, the fewer faults found. Inspecting the top 30% finds a fault in about 83% of inspections and catches about 39% of all faults; the top 50% finds one in about 77% and catches about 61%.
  • The cost view still applies inside a budget. If missed faults are cheap relative to inspections, spend less than the full capacity; if they are expensive, no score-based rule beats inspecting everything the budget allows.

6 · How to use this responsibly

  • Scores support prioritisation. They are not diagnoses. A high score means an engine resembles past engines labelled “needs maintenance”; it does not say which component is at fault.
  • Human review is required. About a quarter of flagged engines are false alarms at the thresholds above, and the AUC is a ranking aid, not a verdict.
  • Interpretability and simple deployment are the tie-breakers. With many models equally accurate, a model whose curves a planner can read, and that runs in a browser (the GAM), is the safer choice.
  • Provenance is uncertain. We do not know where the data came from, whether it is real or synthetic, or exactly how “needs maintenance” was defined, and there is no time or engine identifier. Treat every number as a property of this dataset.
Evidence and protocol

How to trust each number

Data separation

19,535 engines in total: 16,604 development rows (train + validation) for every model choice, and 2,931 held-out test rows opened once, after the choices were fixed. No threshold or setting was tuned on the test set.

Three kinds of CV score

Nested: tuning happened inside each training fold (fair). Fixed setting: no tuning on these folds (fair). Same-fold selection: settings were chosen on the same folds (hollow dots, slightly optimistic). Never compare them as if they were the same.

Freshly executed vs saved results

The 99 configurations on this page are saved, verified results from the team's experiment log; they were not rerun (hours of compute). The final Colab notebook re-executes one representative model per family (including the selected GAM), a nested-CV spline LR, the test-set evaluation, importance and threshold analysis, and checks them against the saved numbers.

Which file is the official submission?

SmartOps_Final_Colab_Analysis.html, exported from the executed Colab notebook, satisfies the course requirement (code plus executed results). This page is the presentation version with the same models and conclusions.

SmartOps Final Analysis: Engine Condition Prediction (CIS 508)

This notebook is the executable, reproducible record behind the SmartOps Model Lineup page. Run it top to bottom in Google Colab (Runtime > Run all, about 15-25 minutes on a free CPU runtime). Nothing needs to be installed locally.

What is freshly executed here, and what is loaded from the repository

Every output below is tagged, so nobody has to guess:

TagMeaning
[FRESH]Computed in this notebook run, from the raw data and the code shown.
[HISTORICAL]Read from a saved, committed experiment result (experiments/log.csv, results/.csv, ...). Not rerun* here: the 99 configurations took many hours across several machines. The producing scripts are listed in Section M and in the code appendix of the results page.
[VERIFY]A fresh computation compared with a historical number (the check passes if they agree within a stated tolerance).
Evaluation protocol (from src/common.py)
  • 19,535 labelled engines, six raw sensors, target Engine Condition (1 = Needs Maintenance).
  • Fixed splits from the dataset: train 14,650 / validation 1,954 / test 2,931. Development set = train + validation = 16,604 rows.
  • All model selection uses repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation, 3 repeats, seed 42 (15 folds) on the development set only.
  • The test set is loaded once, in Section I, after every modelling choice is fixed. Nothing is tuned on it.
  • Nested cross-validation (tuning inside each training fold) is reported separately from fixed-setting or same-fold evaluations.
Business context and limits

SmartOps helps maintenance teams decide which engines to inspect first when inspection capacity is limited. Model scores support prioritisation; they are not confirmed mechanical diagnoses. Cost-saving scenarios are hypothetical (the data has no cost information). Human review is required. The dataset's provenance and label definition are uncertain.

Selected model

The selected (and deployed) model is the penalised logistic GAM with 20 splines per sensor. It was chosen because its cross-validation score is competitive with every other family we tried (the differences are within fold-to-fold noise), because it is interpretable (one smooth curve per sensor, additive on the log-odds scale) and because it is easy to implement (120 coefficients plus knots, which the browser dashboard evaluates without a server). It is not claimed to be the most accurate model. The Spline Logistic Regression (6 knots, C = 0.03) is its closest simpler comparator and is kept in full as a separate experiment; it is never relabelled as the GAM.

E. Baseline models

Always-predict-the-prevalence and straight-line logistic regression. All fits use the same 15 folds and keep out-of-fold predictions.

FRESHIn [11]notebook code cell 7 of 2329 lines
def _fit_fold(factory, i, tr, te):
    m = factory(); t0 = time.time(); m.fit(X.iloc[tr], YV[tr]); ft = time.time() - t0
    return i, te, m.predict_proba(X.iloc[te])[:, 1], ft, getattr(m, "best_params_", None)

RESULTS, OOF, FOLD_AUC = {}, {}, {}
def run_cv(name, factory, n_jobs=-1, kind="fixed setting", note=""):
    """Score `factory()` on the 15 shared folds. Stores fold AUCs and out-of-fold predictions (3 repeats x N)."""
    t0 = time.time()
    out = Parallel(n_jobs=n_jobs)(delayed(_fit_fold)(factory, i, tr, te) for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(FOLDS))
    preds = np.full((N_REPEATS, N), np.nan); aucs = np.zeros(len(FOLDS)); prs = np.zeros(len(FOLDS)); fts = []; chosen = []
    for i, te, p, ft, bp in out:
        preds[i // N_SPLITS, te] = p
        aucs[i] = roc_auc_score(YV[te], p); prs[i] = average_precision_score(YV[te], p); fts.append(ft); chosen.append(bp)
    OOF[name], FOLD_AUC[name] = preds, aucs
    RESULTS[name] = {"cv_auc": aucs.mean(), "cv_auc_sd": aucs.std(), "cv_pr_auc": prs.mean(), "fit_s": float(np.mean(fts)),
                     "wall_s": time.time() - t0, "protocol": kind, "note": note, "chosen_params": chosen}
    r = RESULTS[name]
    print(f"[FRESH] {name:42s} CV AUC {r['cv_auc']:.4f} +/- {r['cv_auc_sd']:.4f} | PR AUC {r['cv_pr_auc']:.4f} | {r['wall_s']:.0f}s | {kind}")

def corrected_ttest(a, b):
    """Nadeau-Bengio corrected resampled t-test on paired fold scores (a - b)."""
    d = np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b); k = len(d)
    n_te = N / N_SPLITS; n_tr = N - n_te
    var = d.var(ddof=1) * (1 / k + n_te / n_tr)
    t = d.mean() / np.sqrt(var) if var > 0 else 0.0
    return d.mean(), 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), k - 1)

run_cv("Dummy (class prior)", lambda: DummyClassifier(strategy="prior"), kind="baseline")
run_cv("Logistic regression (straight lines)", lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)), kind="fixed setting")

One representative of each major family, with the settings the project carried forward. All are scored with the identical 15 folds. Both are scored with the identical 15 folds, and the GAM is evaluated on the test set in Section I.

def spline_lr(n_knots=6, degree=3, C=0.3, knots="quantile"):
    """Identical to experiments/models.py::spline_lr."""
    return make_pipeline(SplineTransformer(n_knots=n_knots, degree=degree, knots=knots, extrapolation="linear"),
                         StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=5000))

QN = lambda: QuantileTransformer(output_distribution="normal", random_state=0)
CB_PARAMS = json.loads((ROOT / "results" / "best_params_catboost.json").read_text())
print("CatBoost parameters (tuned in issue #13, loaded from the repo):", CB_PARAMS)

class GAM(ClassifierMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Penalised logistic GAM, as in experiments/batch5.py (smoothing chosen by a lambda grid inside the fit)."""
    def __init__(self, n_splines=20, lams=None):
        self.n_splines, self.lams = n_splines, lams
    def fit(self, Xa, yy):
        from pygam import LogisticGAM, s
        Xa = np.asarray(Xa); terms = s(0, n_splines=self.n_splines)
        for j in range(1, Xa.shape[1]): terms += s(j, n_splines=self.n_splines)
        lams = np.logspace(-1, 3, 9) if self.lams is None else self.lams
        self.g_ = LogisticGAM(terms).gridsearch(Xa, np.asarray(yy), lam=lams, progress=False); self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1]); return self
    def predict_proba(self, Xa):
        p = self.g_.predict_mu(np.asarray(Xa)); return np.c_[1 - p, p]
    def predict(self, Xa):
        return (self.predict_proba(Xa)[:, 1] >= 0.5).astype(int)

if pygam is None:
    raise RuntimeError("pygam is required: the GAM is the selected model (it is installed in Section 0).")

G. Hyperparameter tuning (nested cross-validation)

A tuning score is only fair if the search happens inside each outer training fold. Here the spline logistic regression chooses its number of knots and regularisation C from a 4 x 3 grid with a 3-fold inner CV, separately for each of the 15 outer folds. The outer held-out fold is never seen by the search.

I. Final model evaluation on the held-out test set

This is the only place the test file is opened. The selected model, the penalised GAM (20 splines per sensor), was chosen from the development-set results above (competitive cross-validation score, interpretability, suitability for the browser dashboard). It is refit on all 16,604 development rows and scored once on the 2,931 test rows. The Spline Logistic Regression (6 knots, C = 0.03) and CatBoost (#13 settings) are fit the same way for comparison. A 0.7099 (spline LR) vs 0.7095 (GAM) test AUC is not evidence that one is better: the 95% intervals overlap almost completely.

K. Threshold selection and business cost analysis

Threshold and cost decisions use development-set out-of-fold predictions only (repeat 1 of the Section F GAM folds; the Spline LR comparator is shown as a sensitivity check). The chosen thresholds are then applied once to the test predictions already computed in Section I. Costs are hypothetical: one unneeded inspection costs 1 unit, one missed fault costs r units. The dataset contains no cost data.

FRESHIn [22]notebook code cell 18 of 2315 lines
assert "GAM (20 splines)" in OOF, "the GAM cross-validation run (Section F) is required for the business analysis"
p_oof = OOF["GAM (20 splines)"][0]; prev = YV.mean()      # selected model, development out-of-fold (repeat 1)
def at_threshold(p, yy, t):
    pr = p >= t; tp = (pr & (yy == 1)).sum(); fp = (pr & (yy == 0)).sum(); fn = (~pr & (yy == 1)).sum(); tn = (~pr & (yy == 0)).sum()
    prec = tp / max(tp + fp, 1); rec = tp / (tp + fn); spec = tn / (tn + fp)
    return {"threshold": t, "flagged_%": 100 * pr.mean(), "precision": prec, "recall": rec, "specificity": spec, "balanced_acc": (rec + spec) / 2}
thr = pd.DataFrame([at_threshold(p_oof, YV, t) for t in np.round(np.arange(0.40, 0.86, 0.05), 2)]).set_index("threshold")
print("[FRESH] Threshold trade-off, development out-of-fold (always-flag precision =", round(float(prev), 3), "):")

grid_t = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.01), 2)
def cost_scenarios(p):
    """Hypothetical cost per engine for each miss-cost ratio r (1 unneeded inspection = 1 unit, 1 missed fault = r units)."""
    crows = []
    for r in (1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5):
        cs = [(((p >= t) & (YV == 0)).sum() + r * ((p < t) & (YV == 1)).sum()) / N for t in grid_t]; j = int(np.argmin(cs))
        all_c, none_c = 1 - prev, r * prev
        crows.append({"miss_cost_r": r, "best_threshold": grid_t[j], "model_cost": cs[j], "inspect_all": all_c, "inspect_none": none_c,
                      "saving_vs_best_no_model_%": 100 * (min(all_c, none_c) - cs[j]) / min(all_c, none_c), "flagged_%": 100 * (p >= grid_t[j]).mean()})
    return pd.DataFrame(crows).set_index("miss_cost_r")

L. Final model selection and export

Final model: the penalised GAM (20 splines per sensor). It was selected for three reasons: (1) its cross-validation score is competitive with every other family (it is statistically tied with the spline logistic regression and with tuned boosting, so no superiority is claimed); (2) it is interpretable, because it is additive: one smooth curve per sensor plus an intercept, so each prediction splits exactly into per-sensor contributions; (3) it is easy to implement: 120 spline coefficients plus the knots, which a browser can evaluate without a server. The Spline Logistic Regression (6 knots, C = 0.03) remains in this notebook, and in the 99 historical runs, as a separate comparator.

Reproduction instructions

Colab (recommended, nothing to install locally)
  1. Open the notebook link above.
  2. Runtime > Run all. The first cell installs pygam and catboost; data comes from Hugging Face,
     saved experiment artifacts from this GitHub repository.
  3. The last cell exports the executed notebook to SmartOps_Final_Colab_Analysis.html and downloads it.

Rebuild this page (Node.js only)
  node tools/build_model_lineup_with_code.js

Rerun the historical experiments (hours; Python venv with the extras listed in experiments/RESULTS.md)
  cd experiments
  python batch1.py   # then batch2..5, torch_nets.py, nested_final.py (each appends to log.csv)

Secrets: none of these files contain tokens or credentials. The data is a public MIT-licensed Hugging Face dataset and the repository is public.
